questions.q: Which DMV does this lesson use to measure real index usage?
options: sys.dm_os_wait_stats
sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats
sys.dm_exec_query_stats
sys.dm_exec_cached_plans
questions.explain: sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats tracks seeks, scans, lookups, and updates per index, giving a direct measure of how each index is actually being used.

questions.q: What does an index with a high user_updates count but zero user_seeks, user_scans, and user_lookups suggest?
options: The DMV's counters are broken and need to be rebuilt
The index is the most valuable index on the table
The index must be a clustered index
The index is pure write overhead with no measured read payoff — a strong drop candidate
questions.explain: Every write maintains the index, but with no seeks, scans, or lookups recorded, it isn't providing measurable read benefit — a candidate for dropping.

questions.q: What does high user_lookups on a clustered index paired with heavy seeks on a specific nonclustered index indicate, per this lesson?
options: The clustered index is corrupted
The nonclustered index should be dropped immediately
The DMV-level signature of a Key Lookup pattern — that nonclustered index is almost covering its queries and would benefit from INCLUDE
The table needs to be converted to a heap
questions.explain: This pattern mirrors the Key Lookup plan operator from Lesson 13: a seek on the nonclustered index that then has to visit the clustered index for missing columns.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend changing exactly one index at a time rather than a batch of changes?
options: SQL Server technically only allows one index change per transaction
Batches of index changes are always rejected by the query optimizer
So the before/after comparison is attributable to a specific change, and any negative side effect (like hurt write throughput) isn't masked by other simultaneous changes
It has no real benefit; it's purely a stylistic preference
questions.explain: Changing several indexes at once and declaring victory when things 'feel faster' repeats the exact mistake from Lesson 1 — you can't attribute results or catch collateral damage.

questions.q: An important caveat about sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats mentioned in this lesson is that:
options: It requires enabling Query Store before it returns any data
It only tracks columnstore indexes
Its counters reset on service restart, so it reflects usage since the last restart, not all-time usage
It can only be queried from a linked server
questions.explain: Because the counters reset on restart, an index showing zero usage might simply not have been touched since the last restart, not necessarily be unused forever.
